query:
We are setting up standards-based quantitative SEM-EDS (bulk samples, SEM only -- exclude TEM and thin-film methods) on a Thermo Fisher Apreo SEM with an EDAX Octane Plus SDD, using the k-ratio protocol in NIST DTSA-II at beam energies of 5-20 kV (mostly 5 kV for Al-Si-Mg alloys; analytical lines Mg Ka 1.254 keV, Al Ka 1.487 keV, Si Ka 1.740 keV, O Ka 0.525 keV, takeoff angle 35 degrees). Instead of buying certified mounted microanalysis standards, we plan to use three inexpensive commercial materials as our standards. For each, we need published evidence on suitability, known pitfalls, and mitigations:

(1) High-purity (99.99-99.999%) polycrystalline aluminum evaporation pellets/slugs (vacuum-deposition feedstock, e.g. Kurt J. Lesker), mounted in a metallographic puck together with the unknown and polished, as the Al standard. Concerns: is evaporation-grade purity certification adequate for a microanalysis standard; the native oxide (2-4 nm Al2O3) on aluminum at 5 kV analysis depths; soft-metal polishing artifacts (embedded polishing media, smearing, subsurface deformation); any published comparison of in-house pure-element standards vs commercial certified microanalysis mounts.

(2) A piece of prime/test-grade single-crystal silicon (100) wafer (electronic grade, dopant at ppb-ppm level) as the Si standard, used with its as-received epi/mirror-polished surface rather than metallographically polished. Concerns: electron channeling / crystallographic orientation effects on characteristic X-ray emission from single-crystal standards in EPMA/SEM-EDS (magnitude at 5-20 kV, dependence on beam-crystal alignment, mitigation by small tilt, beam rastering, or defocus); the native SiO2 (1-2 nm); whether semiconductor wafers are accepted, documented practice as Si standards in microanalysis labs; wafer flatness/polish quality vs metallographic polish for low-kV work.

(3) A single-crystal MgO (100) epi-polished epitaxy-grade substrate (5x5x0.5 mm or 10x10x0.5 mm, 99.9-99.95% purity, e.g. MTI Corporation) as the combined Mg and O standard. Concerns: hydration of MgO surfaces in humid air (brucite Mg(OH)2 formation) -- kinetics, layer thickness vs time, and its effect on Mg and O k-ratios at 5 kV analysis depths; charging of the insulating substrate and required conductive coating; whether 99.9% purity suffices; single-crystal channeling concerns same as item 2; periclase vs synthetic single-crystal MgO as EPMA standards in published practice; storage and surface-refresh practices (desiccator, re-cleaving, repolish, bakeout).

(4) Best practices for carbon coating insulating standards and conductive unknowns for low-voltage quantitative EDS/EPMA: recommended evaporated-carbon thickness in nm; why standard and unknown should be coated in the same evaporation run (thickness matching); quantitative effect of a carbon-coat thickness mismatch on low-energy lines (O Ka, Mg Ka, Al Ka, Si Ka) at 5-15 kV -- percent intensity loss per 10 nm of carbon if published; thickness measurement and control methods (interference colors on polished brass witness block, quartz crystal microbalance); evaporated carbon vs sputtered metals (Au/Pd, Ir, Cr) for X-ray microanalysis; software correction for coatings (e.g. DTSA-II/EPQ conductive-coating property, PAP/XPP thin-film treatments).

For each item cite specific peer-reviewed papers, NIST publications, or authoritative textbook chapters (Goldstein et al., Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-Ray Microanalysis, any edition; Heinrich & Newbury, Electron Probe Quantitation; Reed, Electron Microprobe Analysis; Newbury & Ritchie papers) with quantitative numbers where available. Explicitly flag anything in the three material choices that published practice argues against, and give a concise drawback list and mitigation for each material. Note honestly where the literature is silent.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation

        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We are setting up standards-based quantitative SEM-EDS (bulk samples, SEM only -- exclude TEM and thin-film methods) on a Thermo Fisher Apreo SEM with an EDAX Octane Plus SDD, using the k-ratio protocol in NIST DTSA-II at beam energies of 5-20 kV (mostly 5 kV for Al-Si-Mg alloys; analytical lines Mg Ka 1.254 keV, Al Ka 1.487 keV, Si Ka 1.740 keV, O Ka 0.525 keV, takeoff angle 35 degrees). Instead of buying certified mounted microanalysis standards, we plan to use three inexpensive commercial materials as our standards. For each, we need published evidence on suitability, known pitfalls, and mitigations:

(1) High-purity (99.99-99.999%) polycrystalline aluminum evaporation pellets/slugs (vacuum-deposition feedstock, e.g. Kurt J. Lesker), mounted in a metallographic puck together with the unknown and polished, as the Al standard. Concerns: is evaporation-grade purity certification adequate for a microanalysis standard; the native oxide (2-4 nm Al2O3) on aluminum at 5 kV analysis depths; soft-metal polishing artifacts (embedded polishing media, smearing, subsurface deformation); any published comparison of in-house pure-element standards vs commercial certified microanalysis mounts.

(2) A piece of prime/test-grade single-crystal silicon (100) wafer (electronic grade, dopant at ppb-ppm level) as the Si standard, used with its as-received epi/mirror-polished surface rather than metallographically polished. Concerns: electron channeling / crystallographic orientation effects on characteristic X-ray emission from single-crystal standards in EPMA/SEM-EDS (magnitude at 5-20 kV, dependence on beam-crystal alignment, mitigation by small tilt, beam rastering, or defocus); the native SiO2 (1-2 nm); whether semiconductor wafers are accepted, documented practice as Si standards in microanalysis labs; wafer flatness/polish quality vs metallographic polish for low-kV work.

(3) A single-crystal MgO (100) epi-polished epitaxy-grade substrate (5x5x0.5 mm or 10x10x0.5 mm, 99.9-99.95% purity, e.g. MTI Corporation) as the combined Mg and O standard. Concerns: hydration of MgO surfaces in humid air (brucite Mg(OH)2 formation) -- kinetics, layer thickness vs time, and its effect on Mg and O k-ratios at 5 kV analysis depths; charging of the insulating substrate and required conductive coating; whether 99.9% purity suffices; single-crystal channeling concerns same as item 2; periclase vs synthetic single-crystal MgO as EPMA standards in published practice; storage and surface-refresh practices (desiccator, re-cleaving, repolish, bakeout).

(4) Best practices for carbon coating insulating standards and conductive unknowns for low-voltage quantitative EDS/EPMA: recommended evaporated-carbon thickness in nm; why standard and unknown should be coated in the same evaporation run (thickness matching); quantitative effect of a carbon-coat thickness mismatch on low-energy lines (O Ka, Mg Ka, Al Ka, Si Ka) at 5-15 kV -- percent intensity loss per 10 nm of carbon if published; thickness measurement and control methods (interference colors on polished brass witness block, quartz crystal microbalance); evaporated carbon vs sputtered metals (Au/Pd, Ir, Cr) for X-ray microanalysis; software correction for coatings (e.g. DTSA-II/EPQ conductive-coating property, PAP/XPP thin-film treatments).

For each item cite specific peer-reviewed papers, NIST publications, or authoritative textbook chapters (Goldstein et al., Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-Ray Microanalysis, any edition; Heinrich & Newbury, Electron Probe Quantitation; Reed, Electron Microprobe Analysis; Newbury & Ritchie papers) with quantitative numbers where available. Explicitly flag anything in the three material choices that published practice argues against, and give a concise drawback list and mitigation for each material. Note honestly where the literature is silent.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-part question about using inexpensive materials as SEM-EDS standards.

Abstract:
Collocated crystal sizes and mineral identities are critical for interpreting textural relationships in rocks and testing geological hypotheses, but it has been previously impossible to unambiguously constrain these properties using in situ instruments on Mars rovers. Here, we demonstrate that diffracted and fluoresced x-rays detected by the PIXL instrument (an x-ray fluorescence microscope on the Perseverance rover) provide information about the presence or absence of coherent crystalline domains in various minerals. X-ray analysis and multispectral imaging of rocks from the Séítah formation on the floor of Jezero crater shows that they were emplaced as coarsely crystalline igneous phases. Olivine grains were then partially dissolved and filled by finely crystalline or amorphous secondary silicate, carbonate, sulfate, and chloride/oxychlorine minerals. These results support the hypothesis that Séítah formation rocks represent olivine cumulates altered by fluids far from chemical equilibrium at low water-rock ratios.

Abstract:
An electron microprobe is an electron microscope designed for the non-destructive x-ray microanalysis and imaging of solid materials. It is essentially a hybrid instrument combining the capabilities of both the scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an x-ray fluorescence spectrometer (XRF), with the added features of fine-spot focusing (~ 1 micrometer), optical microscope imaging, and precision-automated sample positioning. The analyst makes measurements while observing the sample (with the optical microscope or with a secondary/backscattered electron image) and selecting specific analysis locations (using the precision sample stage).

Abstract:
Electron-excited X-ray microanalysis performed in the scanning electron microscope with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) is a core technique for characterization of the microstructure of materials. The recent advances in EDS performance with the silicon drift detector (SDD) enable accuracy and precision equivalent to that of the high spectral resolution wavelength-dispersive spectrometer employed on the electron probe microanalyzer platform. SDD-EDS throughput, resolution, and stability provide practical operating conditions for measurement of high-count spectra that form the basis for peak fitting procedures that recover the characteristic peak intensities even for elemental combination where severe peak overlaps occur, such PbS, MoS2, BaTiO3, SrWO4, and WSi2. Accurate analyses are also demonstrated for interferences involving large concentration ratios: a major constituent on a minor constituent (Ba at 0.4299 mass fraction on Ti at 0.0180) and a major constituent on a trace constituent (Ba at 0.2194 on Ce at 0.00407; Si at 0.1145 on Ta at 0.0041). Accurate analyses of low atomic number elements, C, N, O, and F, are demonstrated. Measurement of trace constituents with limits of detection below 0.001 mass fraction (1000 ppm) is possible within a practical measurement time of 500 s.

Abstract:
Abstract 2018 marked the 50th anniversary of the introduction of energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) with semiconductor detectors to electron-excited X-ray microanalysis. Initially useful for qualitative analysis, EDS has developed into a fully quantitative analytical tool that can match wavelength dispersive spectrometry for accuracy in the determination of major (mass concentration C > 0.1) and minor (0.01 ≤ C ≤ 0.1) constituents, and useful accuracy can extend well into the trace (0.001 < C < 0.01) constituent range even when severe peak interference occurs. Accurate analysis is possible for low atomic number elements (B, C, N, O, and F), and at low beam energy, which can optimize lateral and depth spatial resolution. By recording a full EDS spectrum at each picture element of a scan, comprehensive quantitative compositional mapping can also be performed.

Abstract:
Electron-excited X-ray microanalysis with energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) can provide comprehensive elemental analysis for all elements, except for H and He which do not produce X-rays. However, the poorer spectral resolution, ~125 eV full peak width at half peak maximum (FWHM) as compared to ~8 eV for wavelength dispersive spectrometry (WDS) at Mn K-L2,3(5890 eV), leads to frequent peak interference situations in EDS spectra. When interferences occur between the available analytical characteristic X-ray peaks, it is possible that one of the constituents will not be recognized during qualitative analysis (X-ray peak assignment), even for interferences of major-upon-major constituents (where “major” is arbitrarily defined as a mass concentration Ci > 0.1; “minor” is 0.01 ≤ Ci ≤ 0.1, and trace is Ci < 0.01). For interference involving major-upon-minor or major-upon-trace constituents, it is much more likely that the minor or trace constituent will not be recognized. To detect such hidden peaks, the EDS analytical software should construct the “residual spectrum” that remains after peak fitting of the complete X-ray families of the known constituents to extract characteristic X-ray intensities necessary for the subsequent quantitative analysis. Moreover, if this quantitative analysis is performed by following the standards-based k-ratio protocol with matrix corrections (for electron scattering, X-ray absorption, and secondary X-ray fluorescence) originated by Castaing, then the raw analytical total, i.e., the sum of all constituents including any element such as oxygen calculated by the method of assumed stoichiometry, can also suggest the possibility of missing constituents through deviation below unity [1,2]. The following example illustrates the use of these tools for the analysis of NIST SRM 481 Au-Ag alloys (nominal 20Au-80Ag). The surface being analyzed was metallographically prepared in the early 1970s and stored in a desiccator. In Figure 1 (upper), the Au M-family and Ag L-family appear to account for all the X-ray peaks in this energy range. Quantitative analysis with pure element standards and NIST DTSA-II reveals anomalously low analytical totals with the Ag L-family and either the Au L3-M4,5 (0.9040) or the Au M-family (0.8382). Note that if the normalized concentrations are used, the relative deviation from expected value (RDEV) calculated as: RDEV=[(Measured-True)/True] x 100% is modest for analysis with Ag L3-M4,5 (-0.79%) and Au L3-M4,5 (2.7%), although the result for Au has a large RDEV value for analysis with Ag L3-M4,5 (3.4%) and the Au M-family (-11.8%). Close inspection of the peak fitting residual spectrum shown in Figure 1 (lower) reveals the reason for the low totals: S and Cl are present within a surface tarnish layer, but the S K-family is hidden under the Au M-family, while the Cl K-family is hidden under the Ag L-family. Including these elements in the analysis reveals S (0.0162) and Cl (0.0105) and increases the Ag and Au concentrations due to improved fitting, raising the analytical total to 0.9945 for analysis with Ag L-family and Au L3-M4,5, and to 0.9730 for analysis with the Au Mfamily. When analyzed at low beam energy (5 keV), the tarnish layer comprises a larger fraction of the sampling depth, and the S and Cl K-family peaks become much more obvious, as shown in Figure 2. Quantitative analysis at E0=5 keV yields an analytical total of 0.9961 and an Ag/Au ratio of 8.3 compared to 3.5 expected from the SRM values. Much higher levels of S (0.0949) and Cl (0.0905) are found. The Ag content of the surface layer is likely enriched relative to Au due to the formation of Ag sulfide and chloride in the tarnish layer. Trace Cu (0.0082), likely deposited on the surface during the original polishing by transfer from a nearby co-mounted Cu standard, is also detected in the tarnish layer.

Abstract:
The accuracy of electron-excited X-ray microanalysis with energy-dispersive spectrometry (EDS) has been tested in the low beam energy range, specifically at an incident beam energy of 5 keV, which is the lowest beam energy for which a useful characteristic X-ray peak can be excited for all elements of the periodic table, excepting H and He. Elemental analysis results are reported for certified reference materials (CRM), stoichiometric compounds, minerals, and metal alloys of independently known or measured composition which had microscopic homogeneity suitable for microanalysis. Two-hundred sixty-three concentration measurements for 39 elements in 113 materials were determined following the k-ratio protocol and using the EDS analytical software NIST DTSA-II. The accuracy of the results, as characterized by the relative deviation from expected value (RDEV) metric, was such that more than 98% of the results were found to be captured within a range of ±5% RDEV, while 82% of the results fell in the range -2% to 2% RDEV.

Abstract:
Teeth exemplify architectures comprising an interplay of inorganic and organic constituents, resulting in sophisticated natural composites. Rodents (Rodentia) showcase extraordinary adaptations, with their continuously growing incisors surpassing human teeth in functional and structural optimizations. In this study, employing state-of-the-art direct atomic-scale imaging and nanoscale spectroscopies, we present compelling evidence that the release of material from ameloblasts and the subsequent formation of iron-rich enamel and surface layers in the constantly growing incisors of rodents are complex orchestrated processes, intricately regulated and independent of environmental factors. The synergistic fusion of three-dimensional tomography and imaging techniques of etched rodent́s enamel unveils a direct correlation between the presence of pockets infused with ferrihydrite-like material and the acid resistant properties exhibited by the iron-rich enamel, fortifying it as an efficient protective shield. Moreover, observations using optical microscopy shed light on the role of iron-rich enamel as a microstructural element that acts as a path for color transmission, although the native color remains indistinguishable from that of regular enamel, challenging the prevailing paradigms. The redefinition of “pigmented enamel” to encompass ferrihydrite-like infusion in rodent incisors reshapes our perception of incisor microstructure and color generation. The functional significance of acid-resistant iron-rich enamel and the understanding of the underlying coloration mechanism in rodent incisors have far-reaching implications for human health, development of potentially groundbreaking dental materials, and restorative dentistry. These findings enable the creation of an entirely different class of dental biomaterials with enhanced properties, inspired by the ingenious designs found in nature.

"https://doi.org/10.2138/am-2021-7739", publisher = "Mineralogical Society of America", issue = "11", issn = "0003-004X" } Abstract: Abstract While much progress has been made in electron-probe microanalysis (EPMA) to improve the accuracy of point analysis, the same level of attention has not always been applied to the quantification of wavelength-dispersive spectrometry (WDS) X-ray intensity maps at the individual pixel level. We demonstrate that the same level of rigor applied in traditional point analysis can also be applied to the quantification of pixels in X-ray intensity maps, along with additional acquisition and quantitative processing procedures to further improve accuracy, precision, and mapping throughput. Accordingly, X-ray map quantification should include pixel-level corrections for WDS detector deadtime, corrections for changes in beam current (beam drift), changes in standard intensities (standard drift), high-accuracy removal of background intensities, quantitative matrix corrections, quantitative correction of spectral interferences, and, if required, time-dependent corrections (for beam and/or contamination sensitive materials). The purpose of quantification at the pixel level is to eliminate misinterpretation of intensity artifacts, inherent in raw X-ray intensity signals, that distort the apparent abundance of an element. Major and minor element X-ray signals can contain significant artifacts due to absorption and fluorescence effects. Trace element X-ray signals can contain significant artifacts where phases with different average atomic numbers produce different X-ray continuum (bremsstrahlung) intensities, or where a spectral interference, even an apparently minor one, can produce a false-positive intensity signal. The methods we propose for rigorous pixel quantification require calibration of X-ray intensities on the instrument using standard reference materials, as we already do for point analysis that is then used to quantify multiple X-ray maps, and thus the relative time overhead associated with such pixel-by-pixel quantification is small. Moreover, the absolute time overhead associated with this method is usually less than that required for quantification using manual calibration curve methods while resulting in significantly better accuracy. Applications to geological, synthetic, or engineering materials are numerous as quantitative maps not only show compositional 2D variation of fine-grained or finely zoned structures but also provide very accurate quantitative analysis, with precision approaching that of a single point analysis, when multiple-pixel averaging in compositionally homogeneous domains is utilized. One such adaptation that has been suggested is the presence of an ‘aluminum gel shield’ on the surface of its body in order to prevent the dissolution of calcitic exoskeleton below the carbonate compensation depth. However, this has not been investigated under experimental conditions that sufficiently prevent aluminum artefacts, and the possibility of other elements with similar characteristic X-ray energy as aluminum (such as bromine) has not been considered. Here, we show with new electron microscopy data gathered under optimized conditions to minimize aluminum artefacts that H. gigas actually does not have an aluminum shield–instead many parts of its body are enriched in bromine, particularly gastric ossicles and setae. Results from elemental analyses pointed to the use of calcite partially substituted with magnesium by H. gigas in its exoskeleton, in order to suppress dissolution. Our results exemplify the necessity of careful sample preparation and analysis of the signals in energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopic analysis, and the importance of analyses at different electron energies. From text 'newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 11-13'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Performing elemental microanalysis with high accuracy and high precision by scanning electron microscopy/silicon drift detector energy-dispersive x-ray spectrometry (sem/sdd-eds). Journal of Materials Science, 50:493-518, Nov 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2, doi:10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2. This article has 618 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses standards requirements for quantitative SEM/SDD-EDS analysis following EPMA/WDS measurement science protocols. Pure elements and stoichiometric compounds are the typical standard configuration. Multi-element mixtures like alloys, glasses, or minerals can also serve as standards, but must be confirmed to be homogeneous at the micrometer lateral scale and have accurately known composition. Spectra from unknowns and standards must be measured under known and reproducible conditions including beam energy, dose, detector parameters, and specimen geometry. For low beam energy analysis at 5 keV or below, differences in coating thickness between unknowns and standards can contribute significant error, highlighting the importance of consistent sample preparation between standards and unknowns.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Testing the accuracy of low-beam-energy electron-excited x-ray microanalysis with energy-dispersive spectrometry. Journal of Materials Science, 59:19088-19111, Oct 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4, doi:10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes standards used for quantitative k-ratio analysis in electron microanalysis. Standards consisted of a suite of pure elements (B, C, Si, Ti, Cr, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Mo, etc.) and, for elements incompatible with vacuum requirements or unstable under electron bombardment, stoichiometric compounds (MgO, FeS2, KCl) were used instead. Non-conductive standards were coated with approximately 10 nm carbon layers via thermal evaporation. The excerpt emphasizes that at low beam energies, surface layers from oxidation and sulfidation can form naturally on materials, potentially compromising analysis accuracy. To address this, EDS spectra were examined as a function of beam energy to assess the existence of such surface layers. Materials showing significant carbon and oxygen contamination at reduced beam energies were excluded from the study. The excerpt does not specify purity requirements numerically, discuss in-house standard viability directly, or provide specific data on native aluminum oxide at 5 kV beam energy.

From text 'donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 23-26'.

J. Donovan, J. Goldstein, D. Newbury, P. Echlin, D. Joy, C. Fiori, and E. Lifshin. Electron probe microanalysis ( epma ). The IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology, Feb 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1351/goldbook.e02006, doi:10.1351/goldbook.e02006. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt discusses two approaches to EPMA standardization. The first method uses standards with compositions as close as possible to unknowns, assuming accurately known standard compositions to achieve matrix corrections of exactly 1.000. However, this approach faces challenges with complex compounds not restricted by stoichiometry, where true composition may be difficult to determine. The alternative approach relies on pure elements or simple oxides, assuming their compositions are accurately known due to purity constraints and stoichiometric constraints. For simple oxides like pure SiO2, purity levels of 99.999% can be achieved. The excerpt emphasizes that both pure elements and simple stoichiometric oxides can be obtained pure, allowing confidence in matrix correction accuracy. However, the excerpt does not address specific purity requirements for in-house standards, beam energy effects at 5 kV, or native oxide formation on aluminum.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Performing elemental microanalysis with high accuracy and high precision by scanning electron microscopy/silicon drift detector energy-dispersive x-ray spectrometry (sem/sdd-eds). Journal of Materials Science, 50:493-518, Nov 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2, doi:10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2. This article has 618 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes requirements for quantitative k-ratio analysis in both EPMA and SEM-EDS. Standards and unknowns must be measured under identical carefully controlled conditions including surface condition (highly polished, not chemically etched), beam energy, known dose, beam incidence angle, detector take-off angle, and detector efficiency. The specimen surface must achieve a very high degree of polishing to avoid topography that can influence measured X-ray intensities, particularly for low-energy photons. The excerpt demonstrates successful quantitative EDS analysis using NIST Standard Reference Materials. However, the excerpt does not address specific information about standard purity requirements, whether in-house pure element standards are acceptable, or the specific effects of native oxide on aluminum at 5 kV beam energy.

Hiroaki OHFUJI and Masashi YAMAMOTO. Eds quantification of light elements using osmium surface coating. Journal of Mineralogical and Petrological Sciences, 110:189-195, Jan 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.2465/jmps.141126, doi:10.2465/jmps.141126. This article has 28 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt addresses carbon coating effects on low-energy X-rays like O Kα (0.525 keV). A 15-20 nm carbon layer attenuates oxygen X-rays by 4-6%, compared to 11% attenuation for a 5 nm osmium layer. Carbon coating thickness is commonly estimated using color change methods on glass slides or white tiles with oil drops, though these practical approaches can generate varying amounts of error. Coating thickness mismatch between standards and unknowns significantly affects quantification results: varying the thickness correction value from 10 to 40 nm causes total elemental concentration to vary from ~98 to ~104%, with oxygen showing the largest variation. The study found that oxygen concentrations from carbon-coated samples were approximately 2 wt% lower than stoichiometric values, likely due to coating thickness uncertainty.

Carbon coating thickness significantly affects X-ray intensity, particularly for low-energy lines. The excerpt provides transmission data showing substantial absorption effects: O Kα transmission decreases from 96.7% (10 nm) to 87.5% (40 nm); Mg Kα from 99.76% to 99.03%; Al Kα from 99.85% to 99.40%; and Si Kα from 99.90% to 99.62%. The absorption mechanism is non-linear due to absorption edges, making it impossible to generalize about effect magnitude. Thickness mismatch between standards and unknowns directly causes intensity differences in detected X-rays. The document recommends that conductive coatings be carefully applied to clean surfaces with identical composition and thickness for both standards and unknowns. For light element analysis, standards and unknowns should ideally be coated simultaneously to ensure matching thickness. However, the excerpt does not specify recommended absolute coating thicknesses or methods for measuring carbon coating thickness.

<jats:p>Achieving reliable detection and quantification of lithium (Li) with high spatial resolution down to the nanometer (nm) range is a major challenge on the path to fully understanding lithium-ion batteries throughout their life span. This paper presents possible influencing factors, such as contamination, radiation damage and charging effects, on EDS analysis, as well as methods for detecting and avoiding these effects. Abstract:
Thin-film assemblies containing an adhesion layer (AdL) or a release layer (RL) with nanoscale thickness are widely used in semiconductors, electrical circuit boards, optical and optoelectronic devices, photodiodes, and photonics applications. Current environmental concerns and technological demands necessitate continuous advancements in these nano-AdLs and nano-RLs in terms of formulation, design, functionality, and durability. Developing these nano-layers relies on understanding their structural properties, which is challenging because only characterization tools with nanoscale or sub-nanoscale lateral resolution can be employed. The aim of this review is to provide an overview of the current techniques and methods available for characterizing the structural properties of nano-layers in cross-section. Emphasis is placed on sample preparation methods, the fundamental principles, advantages, and limitations of various techniques, and examples from the existing literature. First, selecting the appropriate characterization technique depends on the required lateral resolution—it must be finer than the size of the structural feature of interest. A high lateral resolution relative to this structural feature translates to more accurate characterization, enabling effective profiling and mapping analysis. Subsequently, it is important to optimize sample preparation regarding shape, dimensions, and surface roughness, while minimizing artifacts. Combining techniques that offer complementary structural information—such as morphological, chemical, and nanomechanical data—is recommended to gain a comprehensive understanding of the nano-layer’s structure and properties. This is especially important when utilizing 3D characterization methods. It is worth noting that few examples of cross-sectional analysis for nano-AdLs and nano-RLs are available in the literature, highlighting the need for further nanoscale investigations. This review aims to serve as a practical guide for scientists, helping them identify suitable characterization procedures based on the specific structural information they seek to obtain.

The excerpt addresses sample preparation effects on X-ray microanalysis. Poor sample preparation with rough surfaces can preferentially bias analysis against low-energy X-rays. Conductive coatings must be carefully applied to clean surfaces with consistent composition and thickness between standards and unknowns, particularly important for light element analysis where standards and unknowns may need coating simultaneously. Variations in carbon coat thickness can significantly affect soft X-ray detection through absorption mechanisms. The excerpt provides a detailed table showing X-ray transmission percentages through different carbon coat thicknesses for elements like Al Kα, Mg Kα, Na Kα, and lighter elements, demonstrating substantial absorption effects for low-energy X-rays. Additionally, the primary electron beam can be absorbed in the coating, reducing incident electron energy, which may significantly affect intensity calculations for elements with low overvoltage.

Surface contamination significantly affects electron-probe microanalysis of light elements. Contamination layers accumulate from interaction of the electron beam with diffusion-pump oil or hydrocarbons, creating a dark ring on the sample surface. Low-energy X-rays emitted by light elements are severely absorbed by carbon in contamination layers, which is particularly problematic for carbon analysis where count rates increase with contamination layer thickness. Surface contamination and carbon coating can significantly attenuate X-rays of interest. Oxidation layers present additional challenges, especially for sensitive metals like Ti, Zr, and Hf; since these oxide layers cannot be removed, their influence on measured bulk oxygen concentration must be understood. Contamination can be reduced using liquid-nitrogen-cooled cold-fingers or air-jet methods, though air-jets are more effective if the sample resists oxidation. The excerpt discusses these issues in general terms but does not specifically address beam energies as low as 5 kV or address native oxide on aluminum or silicon standards.

The excerpt demonstrates that surface contamination and passivation layers significantly affect EDS analysis at low landing energies. For lithium metal at 3.5 keV, native passivation layers (NPL) consisting of Li2CO3 (~25 nm) and Li2O (~40 nm) formed even with minimal air exposure. The study shows that careful sample transfer methods (shuttle transfer in argon vs. air exposure) substantially affect detected element distributions, with the argon-transferred sample showing higher Li peaks and lower oxygen/nitrogen contamination. The information depth at low energies (R/3-R/2) means that surface layers still contribute to the detected signal even when attempting to analyze underlying metallic Li. FIB cleaning attempts introduced gallium contamination. The excerpt notes that conventional EDS detectors require landing energies above 5 keV for adequate signal-to-noise ratios and cannot effectively detect low-energy X-rays. However, the excerpt does not address native oxide on aluminum or silicon standards specifically.

The excerpt discusses surface contamination and preparation effects on electron-probe microanalysis. Beam-induced contamination rates are unpredictable and vary daily depending on instrument condition and sample properties. While oxidation of silicates and oxides is unlikely, it can be significant for kerogen, sulfides, and metals. Good heat conductors like copper contaminate easily, while insulators like silicon and boron show low contamination rates. For typical geological specimens with major amounts of carbon and oxygen already present, contamination is generally not severe. However, when determining small concentration differences, contamination must be considered. The excerpt also covers conducting layer preparation: since most geological samples including kerogen are insulators, a carbon coating (~20 nm) is necessary. Variations in carbon-coat thickness can produce analytical errors at the 1% level, though these can be corrected using current models. The excerpt does not specifically address low beam energy (5 kV) effects or native oxide on aluminum or silicon standards.

Abstract:
In this paper, zonation patterns of trace elements in fluorapatite are discussed that were visualized using four analytical techniques, namely back-scattered electrons (BSE) and cathodoluminescence (CL) imaging, electron probe micro-analysis (EPMA), and micro-proton-induced X-ray/gamma ray emission (μPIXE/μPIGE) mapping. Each method demonstrates the in-grain compositional variations in a slightly different way. Both BSE and CL provide qualitative data, and the internal textures are displayed in most detail. Additionally, CL points to specific elements enriched in certain growth zones. Qualitative EPMA maps show detailed zonation patterns for specific elements (with high spatial resolution), which are in general correspondence with the patterns observed in BSE and CL images. The μPIXE/μPIGE maps are fully quantitative and the detection limits are relatively low compared to EPMA mapping. In present spot measurements μPIXE demonstrates lower detection limits than EPMA, however, the latter could be considerably improved by extending the acquisition times. There is no significant overlap of REE (rare earth elements) peaks in the acquired μPIXE energy spectra, however, when multiple REEs are present with sufficiently high concentrations, peak deconvolution may pose some difficulties. Spatial resolution of μPIXE/μPIGE images is not sufficiently high to reflect minor textural features, which also result from the greater interaction depth of the proton beam. However, major growth zones are distinguishable. Even though each method has their advantages and limitations, when applied together, they provide an almost complete characterization of compositional variability in trace-element-bearing minerals.

## pqac-00000021

From text 'krishnan1988atomicsiteand pages 8-9'.

Kannan M. Krishnan. Atomic site and species determinations using channeling and related effects in analytical electron microscopy. Ultramicroscopy, 24:125-141, Jan 1988. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3991(88)90306-3, doi:10.1016/0304-3991(88)90306-3. This article has 42 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt discusses orientation-dependent X-ray emission calculations in crystalline materials using analytical electron microscopy. The study demonstrates that channeling effects produce strong orientation dependence under specific systematic excitation conditions (e.g., g=121), with X-ray intensity varying significantly depending on crystallographic site occupations. For garnet structures, calculations predicted enhancement for dodecahedral site substitutions, decreased signals for tetrahedral site substitutions, and insensitivity for octahedral occupations. However, using other g vectors and planar-channeling conditions, the emission product becomes insensitive to both site occupations and incident-beam orientations. Experimental work on yttrium iron garnet (YIG) with rare-earth dopants at specific orientations was conducted to verify these predictions. The excerpt focuses on how to exploit channeling effects for site determination rather than how to mitigate them.

From text 'krishnan1988atomicsiteand pages 2-3'.

Kannan M. Krishnan. Atomic site and species determinations using channeling and related effects in analytical electron microscopy. Ultramicroscopy, 24:125-141, Jan 1988. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3991(88)90306-3, doi:10.1016/0304-3991(88)90306-3. This article has 42 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses channeling-enhanced microanalysis (CEM) and demonstrates that characteristic X-ray intensities vary with crystal orientation. When the incident electron beam orientation changes relative to the crystallographic planes, the intensities of individual X-ray peaks change, providing sensitivity to atomic site distributions. The document indicates that different favorable orientations produce different X-ray emission patterns—maximizing Bloch waves on different crystallographic planes yields concomitant increases for elements occupying specific sites. A mitigation strategy mentioned is using reference signals from atoms with known distribution in the host crystal lattice; this reference emission is proportional to the thickness-averaged electron intensity on specific crystallographic planes. However, the excerpt does not provide quantitative magnitude values or specific percentages describing the degree of X-ray yield variation with orientation.

From text 'krishnan1988atomicsiteand pages 9-11'.

Kannan M. Krishnan. Atomic site and species determinations using channeling and related effects in analytical electron microscopy. Ultramicroscopy, 24:125-141, Jan 1988. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3991(88)90306-3, doi:10.1016/0304-3991(88)90306-3. This article has 42 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes electron channeling effects on X-ray intensity in analytical electron microscopy. It demonstrates that characteristic X-ray production shows orientation dependence, with much higher effects in zone-axis orientation compared to planar-channeling orientation. The study collected X-ray spectra at six different beam orientations to characterize this dependence. The technique uses planar-channeling conditions that are crystallographic-site sensitive to determine atomic site occupancies. However, the excerpt does not provide specific quantitative values for the magnitude of channeling effects or mitigation strategies for EPMA applications. The focus is on using channeling as an analytical tool rather than treating it as an artifact to be corrected.

From text 'krishnan1988atomicsiteand pages 11-12'.

Kannan M. Krishnan. Atomic site and species determinations using channeling and related effects in analytical electron microscopy. Ultramicroscopy, 24:125-141, Jan 1988. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3991(88)90306-3, doi:10.1016/0304-3991(88)90306-3. This article has 42 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses channeling effects on X-ray emissions in analytical electron microscopy. For silicon doped with antimony, axial channeling orientations show at least a factor of two increase in sensitivity compared to planar-channeling arrangements. However, characteristic X-ray emissions themselves are noted to be isotropic, meaning detector position is not consequential for channeling experiments with X-rays - only signal-to-background ratios are affected by detector placement. The text emphasizes that unlike energy losses, X-ray emissions show identical variation with incident-beam orientation except for a constant fluorescence yield term. The document discusses using channeling-enhanced microanalysis to extend detection to lower impurity concentrations and to determine whether dopants are substitutional or interstitial, but does not explicitly detail mitigation strategies for channeling effects in EPMA.

Peak interferences
As mentioned earlier, one unique WDS spectral artifact are the higher order lines implied
by Bragg’s law in which a higher energy line can diffract at the same wavelength.
However, WDS can in many cases eliminate that higher order line, by fine tuning the
proportional counter electronics, applying "pulse height analysis" to energy filter out the
unwanted x-rays since the higher order lines, although of similar wavelength are much
higher in energy. In the case of some primary (n=1) overlapping lines, even for WDS,correction for spectral interference may be required, e.g. for V Ka in the presence of
abundant Ti (Kb interference) or for B Ka in the presence of abundant Mo (M-line
interference).

Here is an EDS spectra, of an unknown ore mineral, again acquired with a pulse
processing time configured for maximum energy resolution.

Ore mineral (EDS)





Not a very pretty picture, since we cannot separate the Pb Lα and As Kα peaks or the Pb
Mα and S kα peaks. From a qualitative viewpoint we can only state that it is at least
evident that that As is present from the appearance of the As Lα line and Pb likely present
from the appearance of the secondary L lines, although S is interfered strongly by the Pb
Mα line and can only be inferred by the mineralogy.

Here now we have the same ore mineral sample, and it's spectra acquired in the vicinity of
the Pb Lα and As Kα lines, using a WD spectrometer equipped with an LiF analyzing

Qualitative Analysis
Qualitative analysis is the identification of the elements present in the specimen. No
attempt is generally made to estimate concentrations other than major, minor, trace
although even this can be difficult in many cases due to large differences in absorption
between the various x-ray lines.Quantitative analyses (Theoretical Basis)
The first attempt to quantify the production of x-rays in materials was made in 1951 by
Raymond Castaing, as his Ph.D. thesis at the University of Paris. Castaing proposed first,
utilizing a standard along with the unknown specimen, for purpose of determining the
ratio of x-ray intensities in order to eliminate calibrations pertaining to spectrometer
efficiency, and second, that the ratio of those intensities could be scaled to elemental mass
fraction within the specimen, seen here:

                           ciu    I iu                              =                                                         s                                                                   s                                            (1)
                            ci     I i

Now let’s consider, for a moment, atomic fraction averaging as a basis for modeling
electron-solid interactions, which at first might seem more reasonable, although, it is
evident to everyone that has worked in this area, that simple atomic fraction utterly fails to
accurately describe the proportion of x-ray production contributed by the various atoms in
a compound. Why is this?

Figure 4





In this figure, adapted from Reed (1993), we schematically depict the penetration effect of
the incident electron beam for a binary compound, where we have a low Z element here, a
high Z element here, and in the center, a compound consisting of equal numbers of low Z
and high Z atoms. It is evident, by simply comparing the number of colored circles within
the interaction volumes, that the compound will contain almost as many atoms of the high
Z element, as it’s pure element, but only a small fraction of the low Z element, compared
to it’s pure element.

Because of this disproportionality, Reed postulated that the electron beam penetrates an
interaction volume of constant mass for compounds of different composition. In fact, this
is only approximately true because the proportion of atomic weight (i.e., mass) to atomic
number (electron interactions) or A/Z, is approximately a constant, because from isotope
studies, it is known that the neutron has no effect on electron solid interactions at these
energies.In any case, a significant complication arises because we are dealing with a "thick"
specimen (more than a few microns thick): absorption of X-rays, particularly long
wavelength, lower energy ones, can be an important factor in reducing the number of
certain X-rays counted, compared to those generated in the sample.

In addition to this absorption correction (A), corrections need also be made for
fluorescence (F: the generated X-rays may also produce additional X-rays of other lines in
the sample) and for 'atomic number effects'(Z). These three corrections are the matrix
correction, ZAF, based upon various physical models developed to describe these effects,
seen here:

                         k i = c i Z i Ai Fi                                   (2)

Traditionally, analysts have utilized mass fraction for proportioning these inter-element
effects, although as already noted above, mass is not directly involved.

In the past, analysts have attempted to improve the accuracy of their analyses by selecting
standards that are similar in composition to the unknowns, so that there are no large
extrapolations. However, do to improvements in the algorithms used for calculation of
matrix effects, the use of poorly characterized standards now produce the largest errors.
To avoid that, we often utilize, whenever possible, pure element or simple oxide standards
(MgO, Al2O3, SiO2, TiO2, etc.) that have a known stoichiometric composition.

Standards of this type may not always be possible to obtain (e.g., Na2O, K2O), and in
those cases, and for the purposes of using secondary standards as a check on the quality of
the analyses, we can utilize standards whose compositions have been determined by
classical wet-chemistry or other gravimetric techniques, and that similar in composition to
the unknown.

Absorption Correction
Absorption is often the largest correction made to the x-ray intensities in quantitative
microanalysis and therefore the accuracy with which we calculate the correction most
directly influences the accuracy of the quantitative results that we may obtain. The
absorption is defined as the absorption of an x-ray by the atoms present in the sample

Traditionally absorption is considered a one of the terms in the ZAF correction, but within
the last few decades much work has been done to describe the absorption correction as a
function of the depth distribution of the generated x-rays within the sample. Therefore
both factors for x-ray absorption and electron scattering (electron and energy loss) are
considered at the same time. This is called the φρz curve method.

In either case, the most important parameters for the correction are

1. incident electron energy
2. x-ray takeoff angle3. mass absorption coefficients

Th incident energy of the electron beam can be determined by careful measurements of the
continuum in the region where the overvoltage approaches zero also known as the Duane-
Hunt limit. Use of this technique can d

## pqac-00000030

From text 'ohfuji2015edsquantificationof pages 1-2'.

Hiroaki OHFUJI and Masashi YAMAMOTO. Eds quantification of light elements using osmium surface coating. Journal of Mineralogical and Petrological Sciences, 110:189-195, Jan 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.2465/jmps.141126, doi:10.2465/jmps.141126. This article has 28 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses carbon coating for EPMA analysis of insulating materials. Carbon is preferred for quantitative analysis due to its low atomic number and minimal attenuation of characteristic X-rays. The study employed a 15-20 nm carbon coating thickness, which was measured using surface color change on glass slides and white tiles with an oil drop reference kit from JEOL. The excerpt mentions that gold and platinum coatings are less suitable for quantitative analysis despite being used for rough or porous samples, due to their high X-ray attenuation characteristics. However, the article primarily advocates for osmium coating (5 nm) as an alternative, noting that carbon-coated samples yielded oxygen concentration values several wt% lower than stoichiometry due to uncertainty in actual coating thickness and absorption correction errors.

## pqac-00000031

From text 'bustin1996electronprobemicroanalysisof pages 12-14'.

R.M. Bustin, M. Mastalerz, and M. Raudsepp. Electron-probe microanalysis of light elements in coal and other kerogen. International Journal of Coal Geology, 32:5-30, Dec 1996. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0166-5162(96)00028-6, doi:10.1016/s0166-5162(96)00028-6. This article has 35 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses carbon coating practices for EPMA analysis of insulating kerogen samples. Best practices include coating standards together with samples to ensure similar coat thickness, or using a calibrated coater to achieve approximately equal thickness on both. easily removed by exposing the sample to deionized water for 2 min. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the presence of iron
dopants slows the reaction rate of MgO, indicating that MgO without incorporated iron  is preferable for mineral looping
